query: Starting from a multi-element automotive alloy catalyst containing multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios, what single intervention could overcome activity loss and durability limitations while maintaining low platinum-group-metal consumption during transient and low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operation, including exposure to H2O and NO and degradation associated with thermal aging or increasing mileage? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the untreated starting catalyst, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A brief nitrogen‐oxygen plasma treatment can form an ultrathin, self‐passivating nitride–oxide hybrid layer on a multi‐element automotive alloy catalyst, which effectively preserves its Pt‐rich active surface under cyclic low‐temperature, transient exhaust conditions (with H2O and NO exposure) and thermal aging, thereby overcoming activity loss and durability limitations while keeping platinum usage low.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi‐element automotive alloy catalyst containing nearly equiatomic ratios of platinum‐group metals and other transition metals.
generation.intervention: A single, low‐energy nitrogen–oxygen plasma treatment applied post‐synthesis.
generation.conditions: Catalyst testing under simulated automotive exhaust conditions that mimic transient and low‐temperature operation with cyclic exposure to H2O and NO, combined with accelerated thermal aging and mileage simulation.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultrathin, conformal nitride–oxide passivating surface layer that reinforces the Pt‐rich shell by establishing multiple stable metal–(N,O) bonds.
generation.mechanism: The plasma treatment induces an atomic-scale surface reorganization, leading to the formation of robust M–N and M–O bonds that effectively suppress metal leaching, inhibit nanoparticle coalescence, and counteract degradation under repeated redox and corrosive exhaust cycling. This protective layer maintains the desired electronic structure by preserving the Pt-rich active sites despite harsh operating conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated catalysts, the plasma‐treated catalyst will show significantly lower degradation in catalytic activity (for example, lower increases in overpotential and maintained turnover frequencies) under simulated transient low-temperature exhaust conditions and during accelerated thermal aging, while using a minimal amount of platinum.
generation.baseline: The performance and structural stability of the untreated multi‐element alloy catalyst subjected to the same simulated exhaust conditions.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to be observed under realistic transient, low‐temperature automotive exhaust atmospheres (below approximately 500 °C) with cyclic H2O and NO exposures and simulated high mileage (e.g., 30,000 cycles), but may not hold at extreme high-temperature or overly reducing/oxidizing conditions outside typical gasoline or hybrid exhaust regimes.
generation.uncertainty: While studies such as PMC10859931 (showing the durability benefits of nitrogen doping) and PMC10466320 (demonstrating reversible structural changes in HEA clusters under alternating NO and H2) support the concept of modifying catalyst surfaces to improve stability, no prior work has directly assessed the impact of a nitrogen–oxygen plasma treatment on HEA catalysts under realistic automotive transient exhaust conditions. The new aspect here is applying plasma‐induced surface modification to generate a protective hybrid layer specifically aimed at mitigating degradation from H2O and NO exposure in real‐world exhaust environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multi-element automotive alloy catalyst samples: one set receives the nitrogen–oxygen plasma treatment and the other remains untreated. Expose both sets to a laboratory-simulated automotive exhaust environment that includes transient low-temperature operation with cyclic H2O and NO exposure as well as accelerated thermal aging to simulate high mileage (e.g., 30,000 cycles).
measurements: Catalytic performance metrics (e.g., turnover frequency, overpotential shifts) before and after cyclic aging
Surface chemical state and composition analysis using XPS and TEM/EDS to verify the formation and integrity of the nitride–oxide layer
Quantitative assessment of platinum-group metal leaching or migration via ICP-MS or similar techniques
Monitoring changes in nanoparticle size and dispersion over the test cycles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the plasma-treated catalyst does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in activity retention, lower platinum leaching, and maintained nanoparticle integrity relative to untreated catalysts under identical simulated exhaust conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

We successfully synthesized the N–Pt/HEA catalyst with a Pt-rich shell and a high entropy alloy PtCoFeNiCu core with multiple M–N bonds via a facile thermal annealing process and an acid-etching de-alloying strategy. The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst possesses a unique structure and electrochemical stability, resulting in excellent long-term durability under HDV conditions. Detailed studies on atomic structure utilizing in situ synchrotron XRD and XAS, coupled with HAADF-STEM/EDS and DFT calculations, allowed the elucidation of influencing factors on the catalytic properties and performance of the novel catalyst. The high performance of N–Pt/HEA/C originates from the combined effect of high entropy, multiple M-N bonds, and a Pt-rich shell. In addition to the enhancement of corrosion resistance, the M–N bonds through N-doping can boost the activity and durability of the electrocatalyst by the distortion effect in the core structure. The synergy between the three factors further endows the N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst to outperform the state-of-the-art Pt/C electrocatalysts and most binary/ternary Pt-based catalysts for the ORR. We report the synthesis of high-entropy-alloy (HEA) nanoparticles (NPs) consisting of five platinum group metals (Ru, Rh, Pd, Ir and Pt) through a facile one-pot polyol process. We investigated the electronic structure of HEA NPs using hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, which is the first direct observation of the electronic structure of HEA NPs. Significantly, the HEA NPs possessed a broad valence band spectrum without any obvious peaks. This implies that the HEA NPs have random atomic configurations leading to a variety of local electronic structures. We examined the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and observed a remarkably high HER activity on HEA NPs. At an overpotential of 25 mV, the turnover frequencies of HEA NPs were 9.5 and 7.8 times higher than those of a commercial Pt catalyst in 0.05 M H2SO4 and 1.0 M KOH electrolytes, respectively. Moreover, the HEA NPs showed almost no loss during a cycling test and were much more stable than the commercial Pt catalyst. Our findings on HEA NPs may provide a new paradigm for the design of catalysts. The TOF values of IrPdPtRhRu HEA NPs in both acidic and alkaline solutions are very high and do not follow d-band centre theory as expected.
